kraken.name: Kraken Robotics
kraken.locationNote: The map record is a city-level reference. The refreshed footprint text names Mount Pearl and Dartmouth; it is not an exact-site map.
kraken.role: Subsea sensing, power and systems integration
kraken.lead: Seabed imaging, underwater-vehicle power and mine-countermeasure integration. Kraken develops KATFISH towed sonar, vehicle-integrated SAS and SeaPower batteries, alongside subsea survey services. The expanded corporate group and its individual delivery responsibilities remain distinct.
kraken.description:
Kraken Robotics works across two connected problems in underwater operations: seeing the seabed clearly and supplying power to the vehicles doing the work. Its Canadian business develops KATFISH towed sonar, synthetic-aperture sonar payloads for underwater vehicles and SeaPower batteries, alongside subsea survey services.

It also acts as an integrator. The Royal Canadian Navy’s Remote Minehunting and Disposal System programme brings Kraken sonar together with partner vehicles, disposal systems and transportable command and handling equipment. The July 2026 acquisition of Covelya expanded the corporate group; that does not make every subsidiary product part of a single Kraken-built system.
kraken.operating:
Getting useful sonar imagery ashore involves more than the sensor. KATFISH combines an actively stabilized towbody with a winch, tow cable, launch-and-recovery equipment and topside processing. The data sheet specifies a gigabit Ethernet connection and 28 TB of storage, with exports including XTF and GeoTIFF. Those interfaces matter when the survey has to fit an existing vessel, command centre or analysis workflow.

Kraken’s Q1 2026 SEFINE RD-22 demonstration joins several of these pieces: autonomous handling, 3 cm imagery at a reported 200 m per side, and a live feed for operators ashore to classify contacts. The company also reports a November 2025 ARCIMS demonstration. A later MOU proposes mission-planning integration and automatic target recognition; the proposed development should not be confused with what operators demonstrated.

The vehicle and mission still determine the usable envelope. KATFISH literature differs between 5–25 m and 5–30 m survey-altitude descriptions, and its maximum specifications are conditional on operating conditions. An integration discussion needs the selected towbody, handling arrangement, communications path and environmental limits together.
kraken.footprint: Kraken lists its headquarters at 189 Glencoe Drive, Mount Pearl, Newfoundland and Labrador, and a Nova Scotia location at 464 Cutler Avenue, Dartmouth. Its April 2026 results announcement reported completion of a new Nova Scotia battery manufacturing facility. The facility announcement supports a Canadian production footprint, but does not quantify current qualified output or available delivery slots.
kraken.assessment: Kraken is useful to teams assembling underwater survey and mine-countermeasure capability because it spans the sensor, power and integration work between them. The KATFISH demonstrations provide a concrete starting point for discussing vessel handling and the shore operator’s workflow; SeaPower and vehicle-integrated SAS open different platform choices. The worthwhile discussion is about the selected configuration and delivery scope, with Q2 financial figures kept separate from the group enlarged by Covelya.
kraken.current: On August 27, 2026, Kraken reported Q2 revenue of C$27.3 million, excluding Covelya because that acquisition closed after the quarter. It also announced a long-term subsea-battery supply agreement with an unnamed XL-UUV developer. The release reported a C$1.5 million reversal of previously recognized integration-project revenue following a scope reduction.
kraken.finance:
Kraken reported C$27.320 million revenue for the three months ended June 30, 2026, before Covelya joined the group. The quarter included a C$1.5 million reversal of previously recognized product revenue after an integration project changed scope. It also recognized a C$6.911 million provision for probable costs in an arbitration over a 2017 supplier contract. These qualifications help explain the quarter without treating a provision as a cash payment.

At June 30, cash and cash equivalents were C$91.266 million. A further C$396.745 million of subscription-receipt proceeds was separately held in escrow. Neither that balance sheet nor the quarter’s revenue represents the enlarged group after closing.

Note 22 records the July 2 Covelya acquisition at approximately C$615 million: C$355 million cash, C$125 million term debt and C$135 million in shares, subject to closing adjustments. Acquisition consideration, reported revenue and available cash describe different things and should be read separately.

capabilities.name: KATFISH Towed Synthetic Aperture Sonar
capabilities.teaser: An actively stabilized towbody, handling equipment and topside processing for seabed survey. Real-time and post-processed imagery have different stated resolutions; host-vessel integration remains configuration-specific.
capabilities.summary:
KATFISH is a survey package built around keeping the sonar stable while the vessel moves. Articulated tailfins and an autopilot stabilize the towbody; the winch, tow cable and launch-and-recovery system connect it to the vessel. Kraken offers compact USV and ISO20 handling arrangements for different host platforms.

The company’s feature sheet distinguishes 3 cm by 3 cm imagery available in real time from 2 cm by 2 cm post-processed imagery, with a listed 200 m range on each side. At the SEFINE RD-22 demonstration, Kraken reports that the live feed reached operators ashore for contact classification. Its subsequent MOU discusses further mission-planning and automatic-recognition development, rather than establishing that all of those functions were already operational.

Integration also includes storage and data movement: the sheet lists 28 TB topside storage, gigabit Ethernet and common survey exports including XTF and GeoTIFF. Maximum sensor figures do not establish the radio-link capacity or environmental envelope of a particular installation.
features: Actively stabilized towfish and topside processing
3 cm by 3 cm real-time and 2 cm by 2 cm post-processed imagery
Optional USV and ISO20 launch-and-recovery systems
GeoTIFF/XTF output and topside gigabit Ethernet
capabilities.maturity: Kraken reports Q1 2026 SEFINE RD-22 and November 2025 ARCIMS demonstrations of autonomous handling and live sonar use. The May 2026 MOU proposes further mission-planning and ATR development. Literature differs on 5–25 m versus 5–30 m survey altitude; platform-qualified operating limits and delivery acceptance require confirmation.
capabilities.availability: Commercially offered sonar and handling configurations; host-vessel integration and acceptance conditions are specified per programme.

capabilities.name: Kraken Synthetic Aperture Sonar
capabilities.teaser: Modular sonar payloads combine seabed imagery and bathymetry. MP-SAS and larger arrays have different depth, range and integration requirements; their maximum specifications cannot be combined.
capabilities.summary:
Kraken SAS is intended to give an underwater vehicle both seabed imagery and bathymetry from the same payload. The family uses configurable arrays and onboard processing, with exports including XTF and GeoTIFF for subsequent survey work. The published integration data also specifies nominal 24–60 VDC power and 4 TB onboard storage.

The differences between variants matter. MP-SAS is the smaller package for low-logistics UUV work: its table lists 300 m depth and up to 100 m per side. Larger selected flooded configurations offer 6,000 m depth ratings, while the SAS-120 table changes range with survey speed. Combining the smallest package, deepest rating and widest swath into a single specification would misdescribe the offering.

Kraken’s named orders include Teledyne Marine and Terradepth integration work. They establish a commercial route into vehicles and survey services; the exact array, depth housing, power budget and processing interface still belong to the individual installation.
features: Simultaneous synthetic-aperture imagery and bathymetry
Modular 60, 120 and 180 cm array options
MP-SAS configuration for small UUVs
Configuration-dependent depth ratings up to 6000 m
capabilities.maturity: Kraken reports SAS orders and established vehicle integrations; its December 2025 announcement names Teledyne Marine and Terradepth. Maximum catalogue values vary with the chosen configuration and operating conditions.
capabilities.availability: Offered as configurable sonar payloads for vehicle integration; processing, data interfaces and depth options are selected with Kraken.

capabilities.name: SeaPower Subsea Batteries
capabilities.teaser: Polymer-encapsulated lithium-ion batteries with cell monitoring and configurable packaging. The published capacity range describes a product family, not one universally qualified module.
capabilities.summary:
SeaPower addresses the space and weight taken up by an underwater vehicle’s energy supply. Kraken encapsulates lithium-ion cells in a pressure-tolerant polymer matrix, avoiding the conventional pressure housing or oil compensation around the battery. The battery-management system monitors cell temperature and voltage and provides telemetry and software power control.

Kraken describes configurable systems from 2 kWh to 5 MWh and a 6,000 m depth rating. Those are family-level options, not the specification of one universal module. In an unnamed customer example, it reports increasing a UUV’s capacity from 48 to 96 kWh within the same volume and reducing weight per kWh by 46%. That is useful evidence of the claimed packaging benefit, with the configuration and comparison still belonging to that example.

Reported orders identify real integration routes, including Teledyne Marine’s planned Gavia and SeaRaptor work. Electrical, mechanical and safety compatibility must still be established for the selected vehicle; the brochure’s design-for-compliance wording is not proof of every certification.
features: Polymer-encapsulated pressure-tolerant lithium-ion cells
Integrated per-cell temperature and voltage monitoring
Parallel operation and software-controlled power
Brochure configurations span 2 kWh to 5 MWh
capabilities.maturity: Kraken reports orders for SeaPower, including named Teledyne integration plans, and an unnamed UUV capacity/weight example. The sheet describes pressure testing and design for UN 38.3, IEC, DNV and NAVSEA compliance; it does not establish certification or accepted performance for every configuration.
capabilities.availability: Offered in configurable modules and integrated battery systems; electrical, packaging and qualification scope require agreement.

capabilities.name: Remote Minehunting and Disposal System integration
capabilities.teaser: A programme-specific integration role connecting sonar, partner vehicles, disposal systems and containerized command and handling equipment. Amended contract value is not a delivered-equipment inventory.
capabilities.summary:
The RCN programme shows Kraken working as a prime integrator across a mine-countermeasure system. The original 2022 announcement combines AquaPix-equipped REMUS autonomous vehicles for searching with SEAFOX mine-disposal systems and SH Defence’s containerized command and handling modules. It also describes an initial five-year integrated logistics support programme with options for equipment, spares, training and technical support.

That system-of-systems description is useful for understanding where the partners fit. It is not a current delivered-equipment inventory. CanadaBuys records a June 11, 2026 reduction of C$12.154 million to the acquisition contract and a total of C$33.690 million, with expiry in December 2028. The entry does not explain the final quantities or acceptance status. The original scope, amended contract value and equipment actually accepted by the Navy therefore need to remain distinct.

AquaPix sonar payloads
Partner-provided SEAFOX systems
SH Defence containerized command and handling modules

airbus.name: Airbus Canada
airbus.locationNote: Mirabel is the listed map location. The Canadian industrial footprint spans multiple sites and Airbus entities.
airbus.lead: Aircraft production, helicopter engineering and support, defence programmes and flight-operations software across several Canadian sites. This profile covers a group footprint; Airbus Canada Limited Partnership is specifically associated with the A220 programme.
airbus.description:
Airbus’s Canadian presence combines commercial aircraft production, helicopter manufacturing and support, defence-programme activity and flight-operations software. The A220 programme in Mirabel is one major part of that footprint, alongside Airbus Atlantic airframe work, Fort Erie’s helicopter capabilities, Ottawa defence/support activity and Waterloo software operations. These activities span several group entities; Airbus Canada Limited Partnership is specifically associated with the A220 programme.

The industrial offer reaches beyond final aircraft assembly. Fort Erie manufactures composite components and provides helicopter modification, completion and component-support services. A Niagara spares distribution centre opened in May 2025 supports the helicopter network. In defence, named Airbus entities work with Canadian partners on search-and-rescue aircraft, tanker/transport conversion and aircrew training. The work package determines the responsible company and site.

The Mirabel Tech Hub, launched in May 2026, adds a research-collaboration route alongside established manufacturing.
airbus.operating:
A Canadian Airbus opportunity needs to be located within the programme before it is treated as a general supplier opportunity. A220 airframe production, helicopter composite parts, an aircraft modification and long-term military support require different interfaces, approvals and contracting teams. Airbus Defence and Space S.A.’s Canadian defence awards should not be assigned automatically to Airbus Canada LP or Mirabel.

For research, the Tech Hub names concrete problems: titanium recovery, composite circularity, conductive coatings, batteries and hydrogen systems, and AI/robotics or digital twins in manufacturing and operations. CRIAQ now lists TiReX and CiDAD among ongoing funded projects. A prospective collaborator still needs the sponsor, available work package, IP arrangement and qualification target for its contribution.

May 2026 cooperation agreements with CAE, L3Harris and Pratt & Whitney Canada concern possible future training/simulation, EO/IR and engine opportunities. They do not establish a selected system or committed workshare. Existing programmes provide firmer boundaries: CC-295 has reached initial operational capability, while the CC-330 conversion and support programme remains on a different schedule with separately identified OEM and L3Harris MAS roles.
airbus.footprint:
The group identifies A220 headquarters and Airbus Atlantic production in Mirabel; helicopter composites, engineering and gearbox work in Fort Erie; defence/support activity in Ottawa; and flight-operations software in Waterloo. Its published Canadian page reports more than 5,300 employees across the group and subsidiaries, rather than at Airbus Canada LP alone. The 21,000-square-foot Niagara helicopter distribution centre opened in May 2025.

PwC’s 2023–25 footprint study counts 970 Canadian suppliers in 2025, 54% of them SMEs. Its model includes multiple Canadian entities and worldwide procurement from Canada but excludes direct Ottawa Defence and Space activity from its direct-activity calculation. This is a different perimeter from the company’s general Canadian presence. CC-330 production and conversion in Toulouse and Getafe remain separate from the Canadian sites.
airbus.assessment: Airbus offers several distinct entry points into Canadian aerospace: production work around Mirabel, helicopter engineering and components at Fort Erie, programme-specific defence support, and collaborative research through the Tech Hub. The value of a conversation comes from identifying the responsible team and a concrete work package. Group scale and a familiar aircraft name cannot substitute for that programme’s technical interface, approval scope and commercial route.
airbus.current: On June 17, 2026, Airbus announced delivery of the first H135 for SkyAlyne’s Future Aircrew Training programme, designated CT-153 Juno. Fort Erie completed Canadian modifications; the planned fleet comprises 19 aircraft with deliveries continuing through 2028.
airbus.finance:
In July 2024, Airbus and Investissement Québec announced US$1.2 billion of additional A220 partnership investment, comprising US$900 million from Airbus and US$300 million from Québec. This is historical programme financing, not a 2026 financing round across Airbus’s Canadian businesses.

The July 2026 PwC footprint study reports C$2.2 billion of group-wide Canadian procurement spending in 2025, stated in constant 2025 dollars. That measure includes Canadian sourcing by overseas Airbus entities and is not Airbus Canada LP revenue. The study was commissioned by Airbus and relies on company-supplied inputs without independent assurance; its economic-impact estimates should be read on that basis.
airbus.commercial: Established Canadian production and support activity includes A220 manufacturing and helicopter components/services. AirAsia’s 150-aircraft commitment is an order, while Juno has reached initial delivery. Defence-programme awards, approvals and research entry terms belong to the named entity and work package.
airbus.ownership: Airbus Canada LP was 75% owned by Airbus and 25% by Investissement Québec at year-end 2024, according to Airbus’s Board report. The A220 partnership’s redemption horizon was extended to 2035. This ownership split does not describe every Airbus business operating in Canada.

capabilities.name: Aerospace manufacturing and services
capabilities.type: Aerospace production, engineering, support and research
capabilities.teaser: One published capability record spans several programmes and sites: A220 production, helicopter manufacturing and modification, military aircraft support and collaborative research. Responsibilities and approval scopes belong to the named business and programme.
capabilities.summary:
Airbus’s Canadian aerospace capability spans separate aircraft programmes, sites and legal entities. Mirabel hosts the A220 programme and airframe manufacturing; Fort Erie combines helicopter engineering, composite manufacture, completion and component support. Defence and search-and-rescue responsibilities involve Airbus Defence and Space and Canadian partners, while Waterloo’s flight-operations software activity is another part of the group footprint.

The A220 combines composite wings, centre wingbox, empennage and aft fuselage with an aluminium-lithium fuselage and fly-by-wire controls. The -100 and -300 have distinct cabin capacities. AirAsia’s May 2026 firm order covers 150 A220-300s in a specific 160-seat layout with an additional overwing exit on each side; the Canadian government says these aircraft will be assembled at Mirabel. An order is a production commitment, not a delivered fleet or evidence that every A220 cabin shares that approval.

Fort Erie’s published composite workflow runs from prepreg and honeycomb preparation through lay-up, vacuum-bag checks and autoclave cure to inspection, trimming, assembly and paint. The site offers build-to-print through design/tooling/manufacture work. Its engineering unit describes TCCA Design Approval Organization authority for aircraft options and modifications, and separate component-overhaul scopes. Light-single gearbox expertise is part of the established local offer.

For the SkyAlyne training programme, Airbus announced the first H135/CT-153 Juno delivery in June 2026. Fort Erie completed Canadian avionics, communications and cockpit modifications using locally developed STCs. An August account describes receipt of the first of 19; deliveries continue through 2028. This is a delivery-stage programme, not completion of the training fleet.

The military transport and search-and-rescue programmes have different stages and responsibilities. DND identifies Airbus Defence and Space S.A. as CC-295 prime. Its March 2026 status report records initial operational capability, Comox operations from May 2025 and full operational capability still targeted for 2029–30, with the final aircraft yet to be accepted at that reporting date. The aircraft combines search sensors and communications, including an MX-15 EO/IR system. CC-330 work instead involves Toulouse production and Getafe conversion; DND’s July status placed it in conversion/testing ahead of deliveries from 2027.

The Mirabel Tech Hub adds collaborative research in materials, decarbonisation and manufacturing/operations technologies. CRIAQ’s current funded-project list includes TiReX titanium recovery and CiDAD circularity work. These projects complement established production without supplying an aggregate readiness level or a general supplier qualification route.
features: A220 programme and airframe manufacturing in Mirabel, with aircraft and cabin configurations kept distinct
Fort Erie composite processing from material preparation and lay-up through autoclave cure, inspection and assembly
Helicopter modification engineering, completion, light-single gearbox expertise and scoped component support
H135/CT-153 Juno delivery and Canadian modification work for SkyAlyne training
CC-295 search-and-rescue prime and support activity through the responsible Airbus Defence and Space entity and Canadian partners
Mirabel research collaboration in materials, decarbonisation, AI/robotics and digital manufacturing
capabilities.maturity: Established aircraft manufacturing and support coexist with programme-specific milestones: Juno at first delivery, CC-295 at initial operational capability in DND’s March 2026 report, and CC-330 in conversion/testing in July. Tech Hub themes and collaborative projects have their own readiness; no umbrella TRL applies.
capabilities.availability: Aircraft, engineering, support and supplier work are accessed through the responsible Airbus business and programme. Component/design approvals are scoped. Tech Hub collaboration and exploratory partnership announcements do not constitute an open order book, funded call or supplier qualification.

subsea.name: Advanced Subsea Services
subsea.locationNote: Sidney is supported as a mailing contact and carrier-record location. A current operating yard or dive base is not verified.
subsea.lead: Commercial diving, underwater inspection, construction, repair and salvage from a Sidney-listed subsea contractor. Diver-led work, observation ROVs and tow cameras are distinct service configurations; current equipment and mobilization require project-specific confirmation.
subsea.description:
Advanced Subsea Services is a Sidney, British Columbia subsea contractor offering commercial diving, underwater inspection, marine construction, repair and salvage. Its published scope includes pipelines, outfalls, cables, vessel husbandry, structural inspection and work in municipal water, wastewater and other restricted underwater environments. The company combines personnel and project services with several different inspection and support configurations.

The equipment offer distinguishes a Seaeye Falcon observation ROV for coastal and inshore work, tow cameras for broader surveys where an ROV is unnecessary, and a self-contained mobile diving trailer for repair and inspection callouts. These are separate ways to deliver a job: a towed camera is not the Falcon's sonar payload, and the trailer's diving equipment does not define the vehicle's operating depth.

Municipal diving work provides a concrete setting for this service: inspecting and repairing infrastructure where access, visibility and the consequences of stopping service shape the work package. The historical North Surrey sewer case describes extensive hazardous-environment and confined-space preparation. It illustrates the planning behind the underwater task without establishing today’s crew or equipment commitment.
subsea.operating:
The company publishes both an observation-vehicle sheet and a separate launch-and-recovery/tether-management sheet. The first describes a standard 300-metre Falcon. The second combines a winch, A-frame and garage carrying the vehicle and flying tether, with a stated 150-metre work radius from the garage. Vehicle depth rating, lifting and launch arrangements, and tether working radius are different planning constraints. Surface power and the host platform's arrangement also need to match the selected system.

For diver-led work, the published 16-foot trailer includes a decompression chamber, mixed-gas panel, communications, HAZMAT equipment, video and lighting, underwater cutting/welding tools and 300-foot umbilicals. The company describes surface-supplied, mixed-gas and saturation services, but the undated list does not establish a currently mobilized crew or credentials for every category.

The Summer 2017 CADC feature describes inspection of a 9.5-kilometre North Surrey sanitary sewer and the preparation of hazardous-environment and confined-space procedures. It is a useful historical example of project planning; its staffing figures belong to that period. NTPC's 2026 underwater-maintenance page lists the company among bidders, supplying a procurement-participation signal rather than a confirmed award.
subsea.footprint: Advanced Subsea Services publishes a Sidney, British Columbia mailing contact at PO Box 2533, Station Main, and the July 2026 provincial carrier record also locates the exact legal entity in Sidney. A mailing address and carrier record do not identify a verified operating yard or dive base. Metro Vancouver's award and payment disclosures establish a British Columbia customer relationship, while the NTPC record establishes northern tender participation without confirming a northern operating site or contract.
subsea.assessment: Advanced Subsea offers distinguishable diver, ROV and tow-camera approaches to infrastructure inspection and underwater work. Its technical sheets are useful for defining launch, tether, power and payload interfaces, while municipal awards and payments provide buyer-side evidence for the service business. The next practical step is a project-specific mobilization and inspection plan: identify the actual vehicle or dive team, required tooling and credentials, host-platform interfaces and deliverables. The historical equipment inventory should not substitute for that commitment.
subsea.current: Metro Vancouver's June 19, 2026 committee package reports C$55,598 paid to Advanced Subsea Services Ltd. during the year ended December 31, 2025. This is buyer-side evidence of historical supplier payments; it identifies neither a new 2026 award nor the project or equipment behind the expenditure.
subsea.finance:
Metro Vancouver's 2024 award report records competition 24-115 for Crescent Beach Pump Station discharge-pipe replacement diving services at C$78,700, awarded to Advanced Subsea Services Ltd. on August 13, 2024. The award record does not report completed work, acceptance or payment.

Its supplier-payment schedule for the year ended December 31, 2025 separately records C$55,598 paid to Advanced Subsea Services Ltd. This is an aggregate annual payment disclosure, not a new contract ceiling or a measure of 2026 workload. The reviewed material does not establish whether it relates to the Crescent Beach award, so the two values should not be combined or used to calculate contract completion.
subsea.commercial: The company markets diving, subsea construction, inspection and survey services through direct operations contacts. Metro Vancouver records a 2024 diving award and 2025 supplier payments. Current crews, vehicle access, payloads and mobilization terms should be established for the proposed job rather than inferred from undated equipment sheets.
subsea.ownership: Current beneficial ownership and parent status were not established. A federal lobbying registration covering 2008–09 described the company as having no parent; that historical statement does not establish its present ownership structure.

capabilities.name: Inspection ROV and subsea survey services
capabilities.type: Inspection ROV and subsea survey service
capabilities.teaser: A company-documented Seaeye Falcon observation configuration, optional inspection payloads and separate launch/tether arrangements. Tow cameras are a different survey approach; the sheets do not establish a currently mobilized fleet.
capabilities.summary:
Advanced Subsea's published ROV offer centres on an observation-class Seaeye Falcon for coastal and inshore inspection. Its undated company sheet describes a 300-metre-rated vehicle with four horizontal vectored thrusters, one vertical thruster, a tilting colour camera, compass/gyro and automatic heading/depth functions. The sheet gives a 50 kg launch weight and a 4 kg payload, or 62 kg and 16 kg respectively with its additional buoyancy core. Those figures belong to that documented configuration, rather than every Falcon version.

Sector-scan sonar, tracking or navigation equipment, manipulators, additional cameras, cathodic-protection probes, cleaning tools and recording systems are listed as options. They should be selected against the inspection or light-intervention task, rather than assumed to be installed. Saab separately distinguishes the standard Falcon from the 1,000-metre Falcon DR; the deeper model's rating cannot be applied to the company sheet's vehicle.

The separate launch-and-recovery/tether-management sheet describes a winch, A-frame and garage containing the ROV and flying tether. It states launch/recovery to 300 metres and a 150-metre work radius from the garage, with 415/440 V three-phase power for that support system. The vehicle sheet specifies a different surface power input of 100–270 VAC at 2.5 kW. These interfaces matter when arranging the host platform, deployment system and electrical supply.

Tow cameras are a separate advertised alternative for larger-area visual surveys where an ROV is unnecessary. The company also describes access to inspection systems and agent sourcing of larger vehicles. The equipment documents support configuration planning but do not establish today's owned fleet, installed payloads or mobilization date.

Underwater video, camera tilt and automatic heading/depth functions in the published vehicle sheet
Optional sonar, tracking, cameras, manipulators and inspection tools
Separate winch/A-frame/garage launch and tether-management configuration
Distinct vehicle power, support-system power and flying-tether interfaces
Tow-camera survey alternative when a powered inspection vehicle is unnecessary
Inspection-system access and agent-sourced larger vehicles described in company material
capabilities.maturity: Published vehicle and support-system sheets provide configuration detail but no current inventory date or accepted deployment record. Metro Vancouver's diving award does not establish Falcon use. Optional payloads and the separate Falcon DR rating should not be treated as the offered unit's installed specification.
capabilities.availability: Scope the actual vehicle, payloads, launch system, crew and schedule with the company. Its material describes owned or quickly accessed inspection systems and agent-sourced larger vehicles; current access and integration commitments require project-specific confirmation.

capabilities.name: Commercial diving and subsea construction
capabilities.teaser: Diver-led inspection, construction, cutting, welding, repair and salvage for infrastructure and vessels. Buyer-side records and a historical sewer-inspection case support the service record, not current crew availability.
capabilities.summary:
Advanced Subsea Services offers commercial diving and marine-construction support for pipelines, outfalls, cables, structures and vessels. Its published scope includes surface-supplied air, mixed-gas and saturation-diving services; underwater cutting and welding; repair and salvage; structural and video inspection; non-destructive testing; potable-water tank cleaning; and contaminated or confined environments. The project determines the personnel, equipment and procedure requirements.

A separate 16-foot mobile diving trailer is described for emergency ship-husbandry, repair and inspection callouts. The equipment list includes a decompression chamber, mixed-gas panel, communications, bailout equipment, HAZMAT gear, video and lighting, and cutting/welding tools. Its listed 300-foot umbilicals are diving-package dimensions, not a Falcon ROV depth rating. Company statements about WCB/CSA compliance and coded welding are not accompanied by current certificate or individual qualification scopes in the reviewed material.

Metro Vancouver's August 2024 award identifies C$78,700 for Crescent Beach discharge-pipe replacement diving services. For a historical delivery example, CADC's Summer 2017 feature describes the company's internal inspection assignment on a 9.5-kilometre North Surrey sewer and months of preparation for the hazardous and confined-space setting. The case supports relevant experience, while staffing and procedures for a new job need a current project package.
